questions.question: Explain the purpose of VAT and how the output/input mechanism taxes only the value added, using the sawmill–workshop–store chain.
questions.expected_answer: VAT is an indirect tax on consumption: businesses collect it but the final consumer bears it, and it is one of the largest sources of national revenue, gathered in slices at every production stage rather than at one final point, which makes evasion harder. Each vendor charges output tax on sales and recovers input tax on purchases, paying over only the difference. The sawmill sells timber at R400 plus VAT; the workshop sells the table at R700 plus VAT and, recovering the tax on R400, remits tax on only the R300 it added; the store does the same on its margin to R1 000. Stacked together, the businesses' payments equal exactly the VAT on the final R1 000 the consumer paid.

questions.question: Distinguish standard-rated, zero-rated and exempt supplies with examples, and state the test that separates the last two.
questions.expected_answer: Standard-rated supplies carry VAT at the standard rate — most goods and services such as furniture, clothing, cellphones and professional fees. Zero-rated supplies are taxable at a rate of zero: staples such as brown bread, maize meal, rice, samp, dried beans, milk, eggs, fresh fruit and vegetables, vegetable oil and paraffin, shielding low-income households, plus exports, which are taxed in the country of consumption. Exempt supplies stand outside the system entirely: interest-bearing financial services, residential rental, public road and rail transport and educational services. The test is input tax: zero-rated supplies remain taxable, so the supplier still recovers its input tax and often receives a refund; exempt supplies are outside the system, so no input tax may be recovered and the supplier swallows it.

questions.question: Work the four VAT calculations at 15% and explain the treatment of bad debts, plus the ethics of VAT as trust money.
questions.expected_answer: Adding VAT: R3 200 excluding × 1,15 = R3 680 inclusive (VAT R480). Extracting VAT: R3 680 × 15/115 = R480. Finding the exclusive amount: R3 680 ÷ 1,15 = R3 200. Cost plus mark-up plus VAT: cost R1 600 marked up 75% on cost gives R2 800 excluding, then × 1,15 = R3 220 — mark-up first on the VAT-exclusive cost, then VAT on the marked-up price; the profit is the R1 200 mark-up, never the R420 of VAT. The return is output tax less input tax, payable to SARS or refundable if inputs exceed outputs. Bad debts: on the invoice basis output tax was already paid over on a sale that will never be received, so the VAT portion of the written-off debt is recovered as input tax, and re-declared if the debtor later pays. Ethically, VAT is trust money — the state's money held by the vendor — so spending it on wages or suppliers is spending what was never the business's, and frauds include private purchases claimed as inputs, invented invoices, and charging VAT while unregistered.
